summary: Defines GDOI payloads so the Group Domain of Interpretation can distribute security transforms for IEC 61850 power utility protocols, as called for by IEC 62351-9.

plainLanguage.summary: Electric substations need to share secret keys with a group of machines. This extends a group key system so it can hand out keys the power industry needs.

questions: what is goose in power substations
which algorithms does gdoi iec 62351 use
subtitle: How GDOI hands out group keys and policy for IEC 61850 messages in power substations.

tldr.problem: Power substations send control and sampled-value messages to groups of devices by multicast, and IEC 62351-9 calls for GDOI to distribute the security policy and keys for those messages, but GDOI had no payloads for IEC 61850.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new ID type (ID_OID), a new SA TEK Protocol-ID (GDOI_PROTO_IEC_61850), authentication and confidentiality algorithm registries, two SA attributes, and a mapping of IEC keys onto the existing KD payload.
tldr.outcome: A Group Controller/Key Server can tell group members which IEC 61850 traffic to protect, with which algorithms, and give them the keys. The RFC cannot fully analyze security because the IEC specifications are not available to the IETF.

today: RFC 8052 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it extends RFC 6407.

sections.title: Why GDOI Needs IEC 61850 Extensions
sections.content:
Power substations use the Generic Object Oriented Substation Events (GOOSE) protocol to distribute control information to groups of devices by multicast. Sources also send IEC 61850-9-2 sampled values streams. The IEC 62351-9 standard describes key management for the methods that protect these messages, and those methods include using GDOI (RFC 6407) to distribute the security policy and session keying material.

Protected messages typically carry a Message Authentication Code (MAC) and may also be encrypted with a symmetric cipher such as AES. Section 5.5.2 of RFC 6407 lists what must be defined for a new security protocol: the Protocol-ID, the SPI size, the method of SPI generation, and the transforms, attributes and keys. This memo supplies that information and extends RFC 6407, which under its IANA rules needs Standards Action.

Because the IEC specifications are not available to the IETF community, the RFC says it cannot fully describe the security considerations. Implementers must rely on the security analysis in the IEC specifications, and extra analysis of the combined specifications may be advisable.
sections.plainLanguage: Power stations talk to many machines at once and need to keep those messages safe. This RFC teaches the key-handing system how to speak the power industry's language.

sections.title: The Three GDOI Payloads Involved
sections.content: Three GDOI payloads are touched. The ID payload describes an IEC 62351 GDOI group. The SA TEK payload describes the policy the Group Controller/Key Server (GCKS) sets for one IEC 62351 traffic selector. The KD payload needs no change, but the RFC maps IEC 62351 keys onto its key types. All multi-octet fields are in network byte order.
sections.plainLanguage: One page names the club, one page says the rules for a kind of note, and one page carries the secret code. Only the first two needed to be redesigned.

sections.title: ID and SA TEK Payload Formats
sections.content:
A group member (GM) uses the ID payload in a GROUPKEY-PULL exchange to say which group it wants to join. The RFC defines the ID Type ID_OID (value 13), an Object Identifier encoded with DER. Each OID stands for a GOOSE or Sampled Value protocol, and sometimes IEC 61850 also gives a multicast destination address, carried in an OID-Specific Payload. The data holds an OID Length (1 octet), the OID, an OID-Specific Payload Length (2 octets, zero if there is none) and the payload.

The SA TEK payload gets a new Protocol-ID, GDOI_PROTO_IEC_61850 (value 3). Its protocol-specific part carries the OID and OID-Specific Payload as selectors for the traffic, then an SPI (4 octets), Auth Alg (2 octets), Enc Alg (2 octets), Remaining Lifetime (4 octets, seconds before the TEK expires, with zero meaning no expiry) and SA Data Attributes.

Selectors are repeated in the SA TEK because the key server may return several TEKs for different selectors, and because a GROUPKEY-PUSH message has no ID payload. The SPI is represented as a Key Identifier, is 4 octets, and is chosen by the GCKS by any method, taking care not to duplicate a value in use for the group.
sections.plainLanguage: The first page says which kind of notes the club will send. The second says which rules apply, which code to use, and when the code runs out.

sections.title: Algorithms and SA Attributes
sections.content:
Authentication algorithms are NONE, HMAC-SHA256-128 (HMAC with SHA-256 truncated to 128 bits), HMAC-SHA256, AES-GMAC-128 and AES-GMAC-256. Confidentiality algorithms are NONE, AES-CBC-128, AES-CBC-256, AES-GCM-128 and AES-GCM-256. The AES-CBC modes do not provide authentication and MUST NOT be used with the NONE authentication algorithm. The AES-GCM modes provide authentication and are used with NONE.

Two SA attributes are defined. SA_ATD (SA Activation Time Delay) tells a GM to wait a number of seconds before installing an SA TEK sent in advance, and it wins over the GAP payload's ACTIVATION_TIME_DELAY if both appear in a GROUPKEY-PUSH. SA_KDA (Key Delivery Assurance) lets a multicast Publisher learn whether Subscribers have received the SA TEK, so it can decide whether to activate it; the value is a number from 0 to 100.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules page lists which lock types are allowed. Some locks already check that a note was not changed; others do not, so they must be paired with a checker. It also lets the teacher say start using this code in a little while.

sections.title: Distributing Keys in the KD Payload
sections.content:
No GDOI change is needed to deliver IEC 61850 keys, but they MUST be distributed as RFC 6407 Section 5.6 defines, and the KD Type MUST be TEK (1). Each Key Packet carries the keying material for one SPI, which IEC 61850 calls a Key Identifier.

A key for an authentication algorithm MUST be sent as a TEK_INTEGRITY_KEY; a key for a confidentiality algorithm MUST be sent as a TEK_ALGORITHM_KEY. Key lengths follow the algorithm: 32 octets for the HMAC-SHA256 variants and AES-CBC-256, 16 octets for AES-CBC-128, 20 octets for AES-GMAC-128 and AES-GCM-128 (16-octet key plus 4 octets of nonce salt), and 36 octets for AES-GMAC-256 and AES-GCM-256 (32-octet key plus 4 octets of salt).
sections.plainLanguage: The secret code itself travels in the same kind of envelope as before. Longer codes get a few extra characters to make each message unique.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
GDOI authenticates the participants (GM and GCKS), protects key management messages and includes defenses against man-in-the-middle, connection-hijacking, replay, reflection and denial-of-service attacks on unsecured networks. The considerations of RFC 6407 apply to the policy defined here.

Message authentication is optional for IEC 62351 services, but when encryption is used, authentication MUST also be provided, either by an authenticated encryption algorithm such as AES-GCM-128 or by an authentication algorithm such as HMAC-SHA-256. Setting authentication to NONE with a confidentiality algorithm that lacks authentication is not safe and MUST NOT be done. Setting both to NONE is possible but NOT RECOMMENDED, and may be needed during migration. NONE for confidentiality with a MAC can be acceptable when disclosed data is raw values of no more value than traffic analysis.

Confidentiality algorithm IDs SHOULD be included if messages cross public links without other encryption. HMAC-SHA256-128 truncates to exactly half the hash output, following RFC 2104 guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: If a note is locked in a box, it must also carry a tamper seal. Sending notes with no seal and no box at all is allowed only in unusual cases, and skipping the seal on a box that does not check for tampering is never allowed.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content: The GDOI Payloads registry was updated. GDOI_PROTO_IEC_61850 (value 3) was added to the SA TEK Protocol-ID values. New registries were created for IEC 62351-9 Authentication Values (NONE is 1, HMAC-SHA256-128 is 2, HMAC-SHA256 is 3, AES-GMAC-128 is 4, AES-GMAC-256 is 5), IEC 62351-9 Confidentiality Values (NONE is 1, AES-CBC-128 is 2, AES-CBC-256 is 3, AES-GCM-128 is 4, AES-GCM-256 is 5), GDOI SA TEK Attributes (SA_ATD is 1, SA_KDA is 2) and ID Types, where values 1 to 12 match the IPsec identification types and ID_OID is 13. Future assignments are by Expert Review.
sections.plainLanguage: Every new choice got a number in a public list so that all machines agree what each number means.
